query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multiprincipal-element alloys (MPEAs) for high‐temperature applications, oxidation resistance and material integrity are governed by the formation of a coherent, self-healing mixed oxide scale. In this hypothesis, high-oxygen-affinity elements (e.g., Al and Cr) segregate preferentially to oxidation fronts during high-temperature exposure, forming a nano‐structured, hierarchical oxide layer that reduces oxygen ingress and accommodates thermal strain.
generation.material_initial_state: A multiprincipal-element alloy (e.g., a high-entropy alloy containing elements such as Fe, Cr, Al, Ni, Co) processing via casting or thermomechanical treatment, exhibiting a single‐ or multi‐phase microstructure with high mixing entropy.
generation.intervention: A controlled compositional modification that increases the content of oxidation‐protective elements (e.g., adding 2–5 at.% extra Al or Cr) in an otherwise comparable MPEA.
generation.conditions: Exposure in oxidizing environments (e.g., air or controlled oxygen partial pressure) at temperatures in the range of 800–1200 °C over prolonged durations (100–500 hours), including cyclic thermal conditions to simulate service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A self-adaptive, hierarchical oxide scale that is nanostructured and enriched in the high-affinity elements (Al/Cr), which forms coherently on the substrate.
generation.mechanism: Preferential oxidation of Al and Cr at grain boundaries and defect sites leads to the rapid formation of a dense, adherent mixed oxide scale. This oxide barrier slows further oxygen diffusion and self-heals minor cracks via continued adaptive oxidation. The slowed diffusion inherent to the high mixing entropy further minimizes deleterious internal oxidation, preserving the mechanical integrity of the underlying alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline MPEA with lower Al/Cr content, the modified alloy is expected to form an oxide scale that is thinner, more uniform, and more adherent, resulting in reduced weight gain and fewer instances of oxide scale spallation or cracking. This improvement in oxidation behavior is predicted to correlate with preserved or enhanced material integrity during long-term high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: A multiprincipal-element alloy with nominal (lower) content of oxidation-protective elements (i.e., lower Al/Cr) exposed to the same high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold in environments where oxidation kinetics dominate (800–1200 °C) and the high mixing entropy effectively retards rapid bulk diffusion. It may not apply under reducing atmospheres or at temperatures where phase transformations or other degradation mechanisms overwhelm oxide scale effects.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the quantitative contributions of individual protective elements and how local segregation dynamics interact with diffusion kinetics. Microstructural variations (e.g., grain size, phase distribution) may also complicate the oxidation behavior, necessitating detailed characterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of MPEAs: one with the baseline (lower Al/Cr content) and one modified by an increase (by 2–5 at.%) in oxidation‐protective elements. Expose both sets to cyclic oxidation tests at 1000 °C in air for 200 hours. Perform weight gain measurements, cross-sectional microscopy (SEM/TEM) to quantify oxide scale thickness and microstructure, and adhesion/spallation tests to assess mechanical integrity of the scale.
measurements: Weight gain over the exposure period
Oxide scale thickness and uniformity measured via cross-sectional SEM/TEM
Adhesion/spallation performance (e.g., via standardized mechanical tests)
Surface chemical composition analysis (XPS/EDS) to confirm enrichment in Al/Cr at the scale/substrate interface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy modified for higher Al/Cr content does not exhibit a significantly thinner, more adherent, or more uniform oxide scale (as evidenced by similar weight gain, oxide scale thickness, or mechanical spallation behavior as the baseline), then the hypothesis that preferential oxidation forming a self-healing oxide scale governs oxidation resistance will be rejected.
